solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Squarish half of byre contains bovine

indicators.note: contains says the first piece holds the second inside it
only the front half of the word byre is used, its first two letters

parts.note: an ox is a bovine animal

explanation.surface: A farmer describes a boxlike cowshed with a cow standing inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something boxy is shaped like a box, so it is squarish in outline.

clue.text: Aid for reading part of Bible (one of the Gospels)

parts.note: the Bible is divided into books
Mark is one of the four Gospels

explanation.surface: A study aid for reading a section of scripture, namely a Gospel.
explanation.definitionFit: A strip placed in a volume keeps the reader's place, so it helps with reading.

clue.text: Gas in canon exploded backwards

indicators.note: backwards says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the letters are found inside the words canon exploded

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Gas inside a cannon that blew up, misspelt as a church canon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exploded' looks like an anagram signal but it is just part of the text holding the letters; 'in' marks the hiding and 'backwards' the turnaround.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenon is a noble gas, element 54, used in bright lamps.

clue.text: One embraced by former Countdown host, short and a little porky

indicators.note: embraced by says the numeral sits inside the shortened surname
short says the surname loses its final letter

parts.note: Richard Whiteley was the first presenter of Countdown, a long-running British TV words-and-numbers quiz
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone is hugged by a famous TV presenter, who is described as small and slightly plump.
explanation.walkthrough: Countdown is a British daytime TV quiz show. 'Porky' is Cockney rhyming slang: porky pie = lie, so 'a little porky' is a small, harmless lie.
explanation.definitionFit: Porky pies rhymes with lies in British slang, so a little porky is a minor fib told kindly.

clue.text: Serving hatch, perhaps, where bread may be obtained

definitions.meaning: an opening in a wall between kitchen and dining room is an example
bread is slang for money, and a cash machine set into a bank's outer wall dispenses it

explanation.surface: A kitchen hatch through which loaves are handed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' suggests baking but is slang for cash; the second sense is the British nickname for a street cash machine.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both a small opening in a wall, like a hatch, and a cash dispenser.

clue.text: Entice short-term worker with contract finally

parts.note: a temp is a temporary worker

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of contract

explanation.surface: Luring a temporary employee by offering a contract at last.
explanation.definitionFit: To entice is to lure or attract someone with something desirable.

clue.text: Reinterpretation of Callas by a famous opera house

indicators.note: a reinterpretation rearranges the material, here the letters of Callas and a

explanation.surface: Maria Callas's new reading of a role performed at a celebrated opera house.
explanation.walkthrough: Maria Callas was a famous soprano, which makes 'Reinterpretation' look like a musical performance.
explanation.definitionFit: La Scala in Milan is one of the world's best-known opera theatres.

clue.text: Going up old street in France for currency

indicators.note: in a down clue going up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: rue is the French word for street

explanation.surface: Climbing an old French street to change money.
explanation.definitionFit: The euro is the shared money of most European Union states, France included.

clue.text: Endeavour: learner displays a bit

parts.note: Endeavour Morse is the full name of Inspector Morse, the Oxford detective of British TV
L is for learner, as on British L-plates

explanation.surface: A trainee showing a little effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endeavour' reads as effort but is the first name of Inspector Morse, the Oxford detective in British novels and TV.
explanation.definitionFit: A morsel is a small piece or mouthful of something.

clue.text: Go on law breaking in self-defeating act

indicators.note: breaking says the letters of go on law are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: An instruction to go on and break the law, which would only hurt yourself.
explanation.walkthrough: In football an own goal is one scored into your own net; figuratively it is any act that harms oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively, scoring against your own side is an action that backfires on the doer.

clue.text: Economise ruthlessly embodying Scrooge-like character

indicators.note: embodying says the letters sit within the body of the phrase economise ruthlessly

explanation.surface: Cutting costs without mercy is just what a Scrooge-like person would do.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrooge, from Dickens, is the archetypal skinflint who hoards money and refuses to spend it.

clue.text: Symbol that's represented in sum

indicators.note: represented is read as re-presented, the letters of in sum laid out afresh

explanation.surface: A question about which symbol appears in an arithmetic sum.
explanation.definitionFit: The minus sign is the arithmetic symbol for subtraction or a negative value.

clue.text: Holding area for mail train refurbished today at last

indicators.note: refurbished says the letters of train are done up in a new order
at last picks the final letter of today

explanation.surface: A railway carriage is renovated and finally returned to service today.
explanation.definitionFit: An office tray where incoming letters wait until someone deals with them.

clue.text: Extremely pretty and serene, moving around mountains

indicators.note: extremely picks the two extreme letters of pretty
moving around says the letters of serene shift into a new order

explanation.surface: Travelling in lovely, peaceful hills.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pyrenees are the range forming the border between France and Spain.

clue.text: Turning red

definitions.meaning: a radical communist, one who wants to overthrow the order

explanation.surface: Something changing colour to red, like a ripening fruit or a blushing face.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both rotating about an axis and, as a noun, a political radical or communist.

clue.text: A measure of fluid injected into vein, possibly

definitions.text: A measure of fluid injected into vein, possibly

indicators.note: injected into says those letters go inside the rearranged vein
possibly says the letters of vein may be arranged another way

parts.note: cc, cubic centimetre, is a measure of liquid volume

explanation.surface: A dose of liquid jabbed into a blood vessel, as a nurse might do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' makes VINE from the anagram, and 'injected into' signals the insertion; read straight, the whole clue also describes how a jab is given.
explanation.definitionFit: A jab is a small dose of liquid, which can be put into a vein to give immunity.

clue.text: Speak grandly about new fancy

indicators.note: about says the speaking word goes around the letter for new

parts.note: to orate is to make a pompous speech

explanation.surface: Making a pompous speech about the latest fad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' looks like a noun (a whim) but it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornate means elaborately decorated, as a fancy adjective does.

clue.text: Alarm about cold rarely encountered

indicators.note: about says the word for alarm goes around the letter for cold

parts.note: an alarm or fright is a scare
C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Worry over a cold spell that seldom happens.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in short supply or seldom found is uncommon, hard to come across.

clue.text: Run out fellow centurion, maybe

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for a run
O is short for out, as in cricket scores
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A cricketer who scored a hundred is run out, a centurion in cricket terms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'centurion' suggests a batter scoring a century, run out; here it is a Roman officer commanding a hundred soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: A centurion was an officer in the ancient army of Rome, so an example of a citizen of that empire.

clue.text: Not one Tory abandoning upper-class peer

parts.note: not one means none, no

indicators.note: abandoning says the upper-class letter is dropped from the colour word

parts.note: blue is the colour of Britain's Conservative (Tory) party, so a Tory is a blue
U is the old British label for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: Not a single Conservative politician will desert an aristocratic member of the House of Lords.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upper-class' looks like it describes 'peer', but it is the letter U removed from BLUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A peer is a member of the nobility, such as a duke or earl, so a titled aristocrat.

clue.text: Meat that may be brought home and saved

definitions.text: Meat that may be brought home and saved

parts.words: Meat that may be brought home and saved
parts.note: a cured pork meat that features in two idioms: bringing it home means earning a living, and saving it means rescuing oneself

explanation.surface: Shopping for meat to take home and store for later.
explanation.walkthrough: Two English idioms: 'bring home the ___' (earn money) and 'save someone's ___' (rescue them).
explanation.definitionFit: The cured pork in both idioms, for earning a wage and escaping trouble.

clue.text: Improved on G&S ditty

indicators.note: improved says the letters of on, G and S are reworked into a better order

explanation.surface: Someone has bettered a tune by Gilbert and Sullivan.
explanation.walkthrough: G&S is Gilbert and Sullivan, the Victorian comic-opera duo; here only the letters G and S count.
explanation.definitionFit: A ditty is a short simple tune with words.

clue.text: Dislike constituent of salt, avoiding starter

indicators.note: avoiding starter says the element name loses its opening letter

parts.note: common salt is sodium chloride, so sodium is one of its constituents

explanation.surface: Someone dislikes a component of salt and so skips the first course.
explanation.definitionFit: Odium is widespread hatred or strong disapproval, a synonym of dislike as a noun.

clue.text: Prompt car to wait in line, audibly

parts.note: auto is a short word for automobile, a car

indicators.note: audibly says the word for waiting in line is heard, not written

parts.note: to wait in line is to queue

explanation.surface: Instructions to drive to a traffic queue and wait, apparently said out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: A screen device that shows a presenter the script, serving as an on-screen prompt as a noun.

clue.text: Bug environmentalist with travel by plane

parts.note: a Green is a campaigner for the environment
to travel by plane is to fly

explanation.surface: Irritate an eco-activist by taking a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' looks like a verb (annoy) but it is the noun, an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Greenfly are aphids, small sap-sucking insects that plague garden plants.

clue.text: Edges of iron poles and bars

indicators.note: edges of picks the outside letters of iron

parts.note: N and S are the north and south poles

explanation.surface: A description of iron poles fixed with bars, like a railing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' looks like metal rods next to 'iron poles', but it means pubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Pubs and taverns, places serving drink, are both called bars.
